item.title: Issues Surrounding Aging, Loneliness, and Depression That No One Talks About
item.description:
Many people reach a point in life where it feels like they are sitting alone in a waiting room, with nothing to expect, good or bad. A lot of others find it difficult to say, or even speak aloud, how they feel about growing old/aging with grace, some would say. It would take courage to acknowledge “This getting old sucks.” or even that they are feeling out of sorts.

These thoughts are personal, not to be shared; it’s way too private. One of the reasons this may happen, some older adults have shared feelings and have been denied really being heard, not just listened to. “I’m grieving the loss of my physical health, strength, my spouse, siblings, friends, co-workers, relatives, and my joy.” I feel lost.

Loneliness doesn’t just start at fifty or sixty-five-plus years; that is part of our journey in life. Everyone at some time in life will experience feeling alone. Yet, during the declining years of fifty-plus, there is a change in how we see connections to our support systems. The value of those relationships, as we experience attending the funerals, or hearing of the loss of a relative or longtime friend(s) or acquaintance(s).

It is troubling. When physical and medical challenges increase, it is plausible that depression and loneliness may become a common part of the aging journey, but they don’t have to be. Both can be addressed if you seek help. Life has not truly ended for anyone who has woken up this morning.

Things might look a lot different and less appealing than they once did, but sometimes you need a fresh perspective to see life with a hopeful perspective again. There is a scripture that refers to all things becoming new.

2 Corinthians 5:17 (ESV) “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.” Our mindset has to change. If you acknowledge that Jesus is Lord and Savior, your mindset must change. That is the same with aging.

Why People Don’t See Loneliness and Depression in the Aging Population

If you grew up in a society that condemned or stigmatized things like loneliness and depression, there is little chance that you would ever admit feeling those things yourself. Loneliness was often seen as a kind of weakness, and depression was almost on par with moral failure. People used to gossip in hushed whispers about friends they knew who went to “shrinks,” and therapy was reserved for people with scandalous issues.

Mental health was not a topic people mentioned, except to say what they didn’t believe about it. With values like these, many older people are in denial about their struggles with deep sadness/ depression and fears of being labeled crazy; they brush off any attempt to get help.

It’s easy to mask loneliness and depression behind old age. Depression among people frequently manifests physically, too. It shows in the form of fatigue, memory loss, loss of appetite, difficulty sleeping, and a host of physical ailments and pains.

You might be passing these things off as a part of the regular aging process, and sometimes that’s all they are. However, if you have a general sense of hopelessness and disinterest in life, then these physical symptoms can be manifestations of depression.

If you reach the point in life where you are withdrawing from activities and people, where you spend the majority of your time alone, and where it feels like you have nothing to look forward to, you are likely experiencing loneliness, the outcome of which leads to a depressive mood. This is not a weakness or failure, but something many people experience.

Regardless of your values and belief system, you don’t have to remain feeling this way. It can be hard to communicate with family members about your current state of mind, and often they seem too preoccupied with their own lives to pay attention to any changes you are experiencing.

Unique Challenges That Cause Loneliness and Depression for Older People

You might be feeling like you don’t fit in today’s world because you have had to adjust to a lot of rapid changes; it’s overwhelming. The world changes around you quicker than you can adjust. There is new technology seemingly every day, and at some point, it feels easier to stay out of the loop than to try to keep up.

If you are experiencing the constant feeling of being anxious, not being attended to, what I mean by that is to be seen (facial expressions, eye contact, uncomfortable), heard (are you listening to me when I say how I feel, the words I use), understood (validate my feelings with understanding/ help)

It is overwhelming and lonely to face so much change. In many areas of society, it seems like chaos everywhere, and you don’t understand. It is even worse when there is no one to help explain all the changes to you.

One of the hardest changes to adapt to is when you lose a loved one. If you have lived with and loved someone for most of your life and they aren’t there anymore, that is one of the deepest forms of loneliness and sadness you can face. You may find it difficult to begin living with such a space in your life; a life with its most precious element missing.

If you are grieving the loss of a loved one, you are not alone, and you don’t have to be. Do you fear how you can live without your loved one or that best friend? A counselor can help you process the loss on the journey of grieving. The grief journey is not one to walk alone; you will need support when you are ready to talk about it.

Aging brings a host of issues with it; chief among them is having to deal with a body that is changing, in many ways. Anyone would struggle with having limited mobility, experiencing aches and pains that are unfamiliar.

It’s scary, not just uncomfortable, adapting to new medications and having their independence and wallet impacted by all these things. Ageing well can be difficult for some, but there is help available. “Fear not” is in the Bible multiple times.

Hebrews 13:5 (NIV): “God has said, ‘Never will I leave you; never will I forsake you.’” This verse reminds us of God’s unwavering commitment to His children. He promises to always be with us, never abandoning or forsaking us, even in the midst of challenges and difficulties.

During the changes in our lifestyle due to aging, our hope is that we will have good, positive support. We have to think about what we would consider good support. Preparing ahead of time will make all the difference. Decide who you can consider dependable or not, even in the family, and who is able and willing to help. Guard your heart from disappointment.

Also, consider assistance outside of family through organizations that have excellent reviews. Preparing for the transition of your lifestyle will offer you a sense of peace. If you’re relying on your family for support to any degree, there’s a good chance that you feel as if you’re a burden to them. You may not be a burden, and they would never see you that way if they love you.

Yet we don’t know if they are going to be available. Feeling like a burden can add to depression and hopelessness. That is why we must plan ahead. In our mobile society, many young families have moved away, taken jobs in other areas in the state or other states.

Some families are less involved in their older relatives’ lives. There are few things that are as painful as feeling less important in your loved one’s life. They might think of you regularly, but you won’t know that unless they visit you or call you to prove it.

One of the most unique experiences of aging is a feeling of regret over missed life goals. This is a feeling that you typically only get at a certain age when you take stock of your accomplishments over the years and feel like you missed out on doing important things.

There is a special kind of sadness attached to these feelings, and it’s depressing. It grieves the loss of a perceived opportunity from long ago. Or even a few months ago. You might have run out of resources, motivation, and opportunities, but you haven’t run out of time.

What to Know as a Younger Adult

As a younger person supporting an older family member, there are a few important things to keep in mind and a few practical ways that you can better support your loved ones. The first one is consistency. Life can be demanding, but there will always be excuses until you make up your mind to prioritize someone.

The only thing many senior adults want is your presence. They appreciate your gift of your time with them and couldn’t survive without your practical support. In their last days, all they want is to be with the ones they love.

A practical and straightforward way to support your aging loved one through the aging journey or even their latter days of living is to be attentive and listen to them with understanding. They may repeat the same story for the hundredth time. Their stories and their experiences are like heirlooms, and they have held enormous value for decades. Honor them by treasuring them.

Reassure them that they are loved and a priceless treasure in order to ensure their comfort and happiness. This should go without saying, but it won’t hurt to repeat as often as necessary. Aging family members or friends who are seniors will experience loneliness and some depressive moods.

So much has changed in their physical health, strength, and stamina; with the loss of loved ones and the sorrow of friends who have died, they need to know that they still hold value, that their presence still matters, and that they still have something to impart and teach.

Find out something that they enjoy and ask if they are interested in doing that activity. Allow them to have a voice when you visit. It might be a game or maybe a creative project, like compiling a family tree made of old photographs. You will provide company for them as you craft something together. Equally important is that you also provide a sense of purpose, perhaps even creating something that they can leave behind as their legacy.

Next Steps

Depression is treatable at any age, and it is never too late to get support. If you are caring for a senior or aging family member or friend, you might also need to speak with someone for your sake. Consider meeting with a counselor to share your burdens. Please consult our online catalog or speak with our administration team for further help.

item.title: Mental Health at Work: Everyday Habits for Bipolar Disorder Support
item.description:
Work life moves fast. Deadlines, meetings, emails, and expectations fill each day. For people living with bipolar disorder, the daily ups and downs of energy, focus, and emotions tend to feel even more intense in professional settings. Work demands do not pause when moods change, and that misalignment creates real strain.

This is where professional backing, such as bipolar disorder supportive therapy, can come in and play a meaningful role. Supportive therapy offers guidance, structure, and steady encouragement while people build daily habits that support mental health. When therapy connects with practical routines at work, the result feels more stable and realistic.

Bipolar-Related Issues We Face at Work

Bipolar disorder involves changes in mood and energy that do not follow a predictable schedule. At work, these changes stand out because jobs rely on consistency. Some days bring strong focus, fast thinking, and high confidence. Other days bring low energy, slower thinking, and difficulty getting started.

These changes may affect work in several ways:

  • Meeting deadlines feels harder during low-energy periods.
  • Taking on too many tasks during high-energy periods leads to exhaustion later.
  • Long meetings feel difficult due to focus problems.
  • Emotional reactions feel stronger than coworkers expect.

These experiences say nothing about a person’s intelligence or talent. Instead, they reflect how bipolar disorder interacts with structured work demands. Supportive therapy helps people recognize patterns, plan ahead, and reduce the impact of these changes. Awareness builds the base for progress.

How Stress at Work Makes Bipolar Symptoms Harder to Manage

Stress sits at the center of many work challenges. Deadlines, evaluations, and team conflicts push emotional limits for anyone. For someone with bipolar disorder, stress only increases symptoms and shortens recovery time.

Work stress may lead to:

  • Mood changes that affect focus and decision-making.
  • Sleep problems that worsen both high and low energy periods.
  • Increased irritability that creates tension with coworkers.
  • Thought patterns that turn stress into harsh self-criticism.

Supportive therapy teaches tools to manage stress, yet daily habits also matter. Short breaks during the day help reset focus. Clear task lists reduce mental clutter. Realistic goals protect energy. Simple breathing exercises calm the nervous system during tense situations. These practical actions help a lot to reduce pressure and support therapy work.

What Colleagues Usually Misunderstand About Bipolar Disorder Support at Work

Misunderstanding remains one of the biggest workplace barriers. Some people view bipolar disorder as moodiness or believe supportive therapy for colleagues is a cop-out for people who aren’t smart enough to do their work. Neither view reflects reality.

Supportive therapy serves as ongoing guidance rather than a one-time solution. It supports learning, practice, and growth over time.

Common misunderstandings include:

  • Therapy means problems disappear.
  • People with bipolar disorder lack reliability.
  • Medication alone solves everything.

Rather, supportive therapy focuses on coping skills, emotional awareness, communication, and routine building. Medication may play a role, yet therapy addresses daily life challenges directly. Many people with bipolar disorder succeed in demanding roles when workplaces offer understanding and reasonable flexibility.

Clear conversations help reduce these misunderstandings. When teams learn that supportive therapy builds daily skills, respect, and trust increases. Struggles related to this disorder do not always appear clearly. Changes may develop slowly and go unnoticed. Paying attention with care helps teams respond early.

How To Tell When Someone Is Struggling at Work

Signs that suggest a colleague needs support include:

  • Changes in work quality or pace
  • Less participation in meetings or social time
  • Visible fatigue or focus problems
  • Strong emotional reactions to feedback
  • Missed deadlines or task avoidance

These signs signal stress rather than failure. A respectful check-in opens space for honesty. Simple words, such as ‘I noticed you seem stressed and wanted to check how you are doing,’ show care without pressure. Supportive therapy works best when people feel safe discussing challenges.

Healthy communication shapes workplace culture. Small changes in how people speak and listen make a lasting difference.

Simple Communication Habits That Support Mental Health at Work

Listen without judgment Give colleagues space to share without rushing to solutions.

Use clear, kind language Avoid phrases that minimize feelings, like “Just relax.” Instead, say, “I hear you, that sounds tough.”

Respect boundaries If someone shares about their mental health, keep it private unless they ask for help. Offer encouragement.

Affirming speech Simple words like “You’re doing great” or “I appreciate your effort” help counter distorted thinking.

Check in regularly A quick “How’s your day going?” shows care and builds trust.

Supportive therapy teaches many of these skills, yet their impact grows when entire teams practice them. A respectful workplace supports mental health for everyone.

In addition, supportive therapy becomes stronger when daily habits support emotional balance. Work-life routines influence mood, focus, and stress levels more than many people realize, and it helps when someone pairs this support with helpful, healthy habits.

Pairing Supportive Therapy with Healthy Lifestyle Choices

Balanced meals Eating regularly helps maintain energy and focus.

Movement breaks Stretching or walking during the day reduces stress and boosts mood.

Sleep routines Prioritizing rest makes therapy strategies more effective.

Mindfulness practices Short breathing exercises during stressful moments help reset emotions.

Work-life boundaries Logging off at a set time prevents burnout and protects mental health.

These habits support therapy rather than replace it. Together, they create a steady ground for managing bipolar disorder at work.

Managing High Energy Periods at Work

High energy periods bring productivity and confidence, yet they also bring risks. Taking on too many tasks, skipping breaks, and working late hours increase burnout risk.

Supportive therapy helps people recognize early signs of rising energy. Planning ahead keeps work balanced. Writing task limits, scheduling breaks, and checking priorities with supervisors reduce strain later. These steps protect both performance and health.

Supporting Low Energy Periods Without Shame

Low energy periods affect motivation, focus, and speed. Shame makes these periods harder. Supportive therapy helps replace self-criticism with realistic planning.

Helpful steps include:

  • Breaking tasks into smaller steps
  • Asking for clarification or deadline adjustments
  • Focusing on essential tasks first
  • Using written reminders to support focus

These strategies support productivity without self-punishment. They encourage steady progress rather than perfection.

When to Ask for Extra Bipolar Disorder Support

Even with therapy and strong habits, additional help becomes necessary at times. Some warning signs might be:

  • Ongoing trouble meeting work responsibilities
  • Mood changes that feel unmanageable
  • Tension with coworkers that continues
  • Loss of interest in work or daily routines
  • Thoughts that work or life no longer feel meaningful

Reaching out reflects strength and self-awareness. Bipolar disorder support therapy provides guidance during these periods and helps restore balance. Encouraging a colleague to seek help also reflects care and professionalism.

Creating a Workplace That Supports Mental Health

Workplaces thrive when mental health receives open attention. Policies, flexibility, and respectful communication build safer environments. When leaders speak openly about mental health resources, employees feel more comfortable seeking support.

Bipolar disorder supportive therapy gives people tools to manage symptoms. Everyday habits strengthen those tools. Together, they support a steady work-life balance and personal growth.

Mental health belongs in workplace conversations. Bipolar disorder support therapy offers structure, understanding, and practical skills that support daily work life. When paired with clear communication, stress management, and healthy routines, therapy supports long-term stability.

If you feel like your thoughts or emotions are making you work harder than you should be, or if you notice a colleague struggling, don’t wait. You are in the right place.

Contact our reception team today to learn more about finding bipolar disorder support, or to suggest professional support to a team member who may need it. Taking that step could change not only your workday but your entire outlook on life.

item.title: Social Media and Mental Health: What Doomscrolling Does to the Christian Mind
item.description:
What starts as an innocent look at the news or social media feed to catch up on the latest conversations often stretches into hours. The content shifts from interesting to heavy, alarming, and hard to put down. This is called doomscrolling. It is the compulsive habit of consuming negative, distressing content.

The conversations around social media and mental health are becoming a more serious topic. For believers, it is much deeper than screen time. It is a situation that affects the mind, the soul, and the daily practice of peace meant to be cultivated by faith. This is particularly important when we consider how God calls us to protect our thoughts:

Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. – Romans 12:2, ESV

The Pull Is Real: Understanding Social Media and Mental Health

Scrolling works in a way that appears to be engineered. Platforms are designed to keep users engaged. The algorithms that power them learn to provoke outrage and fear in users. It is not just a lack of discipline, but also a reflection of how these systems are built and the social pressures that come with disconnecting.

Today’s culture leans toward big fan bases and huge numbers of followers, making disconnection feel like negligence. Culture says we’re staying informed, and that means we are responsible. This results in a mindset where stepping away feels like falling behind or not caring.

There is a link between heavy social media use and high rates of anxiety, depression, and emotional exhaustion. It is a cycle that builds on itself. When an individual scrolls more, their nervous system becomes more activated. This results in a struggle to feel settled after scrolling for long periods. Physically, it leads to a mental fog that’s difficult to shake, even though the phone has been put down for hours.

Christian counselors can identify this pattern as a steady erosion of peace that accumulates slowly until its absence becomes impossible to ignore. What may have started as a habit has become a weight that rarely announces what it is doing. Instead, we should focus on the things described in Scripture:

Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things. – Philippians 4:8, ESV

The Christian mind was not built for this

God’s Word teaches about the importance of guarding the mind and instructs us to renew it and set it on things above. But today’s digital culture pushes a more dominant message in the opposite direction. It is an unspoken expectation that says looking away is being uninformed, uncaring, and complicit.

This message sets up a difficult balance for the Christian who wants to stay engaged but also feels called to protect their inner life, which depends on faith. This is a real dilemma that signals something significant is being asked of the mind.

The human brain was not created to process this unrelenting stream of global suffering, breaking news, or comparisons. The constant exposure to distressing content leads to numbness rather than compassion. It creates exhaustion and a quiet kind of despair that settles as people absorb the narratives from their feeds.

The world can reshape perceptions, other people, and even a person’s view of God. The unrelenting, disparaging news does not lead to a perception defined by faith. Instead, it slowly feeds information that keeps us questioning until the damage has already been done. This does not lead to the peace we find in Christ.

You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. – Isaiah 26:3, ESV

How Social Media and Mental Health Patterns Take Root in Daily Life

Doomscrolling slides into the early-morning moments before the day begins and breaks in during the gaps between tasks. It walks into the quiet spaces that once held prayer, reflection, and stillness, and before long, it has become the default. Before a conscious thought, the hand reaches for a phone, and the result is a reactive rhythm of life. The soul is not allowed to be still long enough to find its footing, and there’s no margin left to breathe.

The demand to stay connected competes with staying centered. It builds pressure that is difficult to name but easy to feel. Individuals go to bed carrying heavier weight than when they woke up. The stories and images that have accumulated throughout the day have become lodged in the mind and soul, with nowhere to go.

Christian counselors are trained to work with anxiety and feelings of being digitally overwhelmed. They emphasize that the problem is rarely a single piece of content, but rather the cumulative effect of hours of low-grade emotional input from doomscrolling. The mind was not meant to be consumed by this constant barrage of information. It was designed to be cultivated through healthy and positive interactions with the world and the people in it.

With help, we can be reminded to “Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.” (Colossians 3:2, ESV) This is where we find the peace we long for, not on our feeds or news cycles.

Reclaiming the Mind Through Faith and Intentional Practice

Choosing to step back from doomscrolling doesn’t mean you don’t want to be informed or that you are withdrawing from the world. It is a conscious choice to reinforce the capacity to show up with clarity, compassion, and grounded faith.

By setting boundaries and limits on online habits, an individual can exercise stewardship over a mind given by God. It is an intentional decision to tend to the inner life, with faith that asks for the godly, even as the rest of the culture is still scrolling.

There are practical steps that can make a big difference, such as setting a specific time for scrolling news, removing apps from the home screen, or choosing Scripture and prayer before the first scroll. These are small, consistent choices that can change the feelings and trajectory of the day.

Christian counselors are an avenue of support for this process when anxious scrolling is connected to patterns of fear or a need to control things. The road is really simple, but it is one that faith knows. One step at a time, with a focus on something steady rather than a newsfeed, leads to a quieter mind and a better understanding of what peace should truly be.

You don’t have to do it alone

The digital world and the life of the mind are a way that’s more than a simple lifestyle issue. For Christians, it can be a spiritual one, where the mind takes in and shapes, with the heart, what it believes. This becomes a lifestyle that reflects how an individual lives day to day.

Doomscrolling feeds on comparison, fear, and a lack of hope. A Christian mind anchored in a God who is not rattled begins to understand that His peace extends beyond anything a human mind can comprehend. It is a discovery that His purposes are not undone by anything trending in the newsfeed.

To reclaim the mind takes work that doesn’t happen in a single decision or a weekend without screens. Reclaiming happens in the daily practice of choosing where an individual directs their attention. It is a reflection of purposefully choosing what to feed the soul and who to trust with the weight of the world. This type of faithfulness is quiet and not glamorous, but it is what a renewed mind looks like in the digital age.

In doing this, we can experience the kind of peace we long for:

And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. – Philippians 4:7, ESV

If you feel that you are engulfed in patterns of digital anxiety and emotional exhaustion connected to online habits, you’re not alone. Many individuals are finding the same battle. If you would like more information, you can contact our office today, and our reception team will connect you with support. You can make an informed decision on the next step toward healthier social media habits.

item.title: Understanding Autism in Women: 3 Support Strategies Beyond Medication
item.description:
For years, she thought she was simply “too sensitive.” Crowded stores felt exhausting. Bright lights were distracting. Conversations in groups felt overwhelming, and she often replayed them in her mind afterward, wondering if she had said the wrong thing. Many women spend years believing they are shy, anxious, or “too much,” only to discover later in life that Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) may help explain experiences they have had since childhood.

Autism in women is often diagnosed at a much later age because the signs are either missed or diagnosed under different ailments (1). But when a woman does receive a diagnosis of ASD, there is promising research for treatments that do not rely as heavily on medication.

What Is Autism Spectrum Disorder?

ASD is a developmental, neurodivergent condition that involves significant challenges in communication and social interaction, as well as limitations in behavior patterns. This includes repetitive, highly limited or restricted interests, and inflexibility, among others. The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria were updated by the American Psychiatric Association in 2022.

If you think you or a loved one may have ASD but have yet to be diagnosed, we recommend seeing a licensed therapist in one of our offices to discuss your concerns.

Why Autism in Women Gets Missed

There are several reasons a girl may be categorized as “normal” or as having a shy personality or possibly diagnosed with anxiety instead of autism when she’s growing up.

One reason is that anyone — female or male — who is naturally less expressive will not exhibit the expressive signs of another more overt personality who is struggling with social interaction. Another reason is that some of the research used to set the gold standard of autism measures was set using boys as the model, and girls present differently (1).

While a boy with autism may be flagged for an evaluation because he limits his toys to dinosaurs and stacks them repeatedly, a girl may not be flagged because she is playing with her dolls. However, what a teacher or parent might not notice is that within her pretend play, the girl is also exhibiting behavioral patterns that would signify the need for further assessment.

A girl may play by lining up the dolls and mimicking the same pretend story over and over. The reason the girl did not get assessed in the first place is that her play traits are more characteristic of her gender than the boy’s, and they are less noticeable.

Autism in women also gets missed because they learn to cope by masking their neurodivergent patterns of behavior and mimicking the behaviors they see of normalized social cues. This can be exhausting, and it often leads to burnout (2). For many women, masking becomes so automatic that they do not realize how much energy it requires until they begin experiencing chronic exhaustion or burnout. Many women do not seek treatment until they recognize the signs of burnout and wonder what could be causing their extreme responses to what appear to be everyday social interactions.

What Might Autism in Women Look Like?

Women with autism have similar interests to any woman, but some of the neurodivergences can include:

● Preferring one-on-one discussions instead of group discussions
● Sensory avoidance and sensitivity to light or sound
● Internalizing shutdowns so they appear to be zoning out, but in actuality, they are overwhelmed by external stimuli
● Practicing scripts to mimic the social norms that are expected
● Adopting personas to become like what they think they should be, e.g., an organized student or a helpful co-worker
● Stemming behaviors that aren’t as overt, such as hair twirling, cuticle picking, or quiet humming
● Misunderstanding conflicts, particularly in relationships or friendships
● Inability to maintain long-term friendships due to frustration, inflexibility, or limited interests

While every person is different, autism in women can also appear differently because there are levels of autism. These are some of the characteristics that might help you or someone you love find something relatable and a reason to reach out.

Treatments for Autism in Women Beyond Medicine

While medicines can provide relief to specific symptoms, this article maintains that a licensed counselor will work with a woman to determine those. It is important not to self-diagnose. Some women will have other conditions alongside ASD, and it is essential to understand their entire mental health portfolio to manage all conditions together.

Recent research suggests that a promising discovery could be beneficial, particularly for women (3) who struggle with sensory challenges related to autism. Using VR technology, one small study noted that women were better able to self-regulate when they were overstimulated. The technology allowed them to choose their own room filled with silence, and it did not matter what their physical location was.

This game-changer could be pivotal in helping anyone with autism, particularly in areas where moving locations is not an option, such as traveling through airports or in shopping malls. The research and prototype are still in their early stages, but the findings are promising.

Other treatments include resource-based support, such as guiding adolescents into adulthood by helping them with life skills and communication. An Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) support can help adolescents transition through coaching that’s targeted to their specific needs.

The ABA might include breaking down large skill sets into smaller chunks for practical problem-solving. Practical examples are using ABA to ensure you are getting on the right bus at the end of your shift, or how to answer questions appropriately in a job interview.

Self-assessment and reflection tools also help autistic adults as they learn how to identify their own skill gaps. Then, they can recognize what guidance could be helpful as they seek treatment from a therapist. Reflecting on how they feel in relationships, friendships, or the workplace may help reveal a particular challenge with interpersonal communication.

On the other hand, a guided tool geared toward women with autism may ask about self-care habits, such as sleep, hobbies, and routines. These questions can provide clues related to a need for more attention to broadening interests or expanding routines.

Vocation and social support are also shown to be effective. Especially for autism in women, you or your loved one may have wondered why a specific line of work has been so challenging, and the diagnosis may shed some light on it.

With vocational support and the Americans with Disabilities Act, several companies are designing inclusive workspaces, programs, and workplace roles that enable a person diagnosed with ASD to thrive. Social support may include one-on-one peer feedback or group therapy, both guided by licensed therapists.

Research on Autism in Women

While the research on autism in women is still emerging, the future of support, treatment, and vitality is strong. Several universities have developed programs of study for adult learners with autism, recognizing the need for further advancement.

One recent study showed that clinicians need to keep autism on their radar when women seek treatment for other conditions, such as eating disorders, anxiety, burnout, and ADHD. Some women may have comorbidities or have been misdiagnosed at the time they initially sought treatment.

Next Steps

If you suspect that you or another adult woman you know has autism, there are a few ways you can help. Depending on the nature of your relationship, you can consider the following:

· When was the most recent appointment with her primary care physician?
· What other challenges are present?
· What are some of the past obstacles socially, academically, and interpersonally?

After that, or if you are the person you suspect may be autistic, you can contact a licensed psychologist or psychiatrist who specializes in ASD. Our offices are staffed with therapists who have the appropriate training and experience to help you on your journey to thriving and well-being.

One thing to keep in mind is that there is not one test or assessment that clinicians use to decide if you have autism. Instead, the diagnosis will be based on a variety of questionnaires, your medical and health history, and you will likely need multiple appointments. But the important part is that you will have access to support once you are diagnosed — whether you have autism or not.

Take the first step and reach out for an initial evaluation. In the meantime, you can read articles about autism spectrum disorder and watch videos of other adults who were diagnosed later in life. It may encourage you to hear about their stories, so you will be informed, educated, and motivated for the path ahead.

Autism in women is often more complex to assess than in men, especially during childhood and adolescence. If you relate to anything you’ve read here, it is wise to seek an expert opinion. Contact an office near you today.

item.title: Understanding and Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma
item.description:
Can we ever truly escape the past? Sometimes it can feel as though the past repeats itself, and its chains have us in an iron grip we cannot release ourselves from.

It can be daunting to look at your own past and see the ways it reaches into your present. Wounds from the past, such as intergenerational trauma, can influence your day-to-day patterns and behavior. The good news is that the future is an open vista, and lasting healing is a real possibility.

Intergenerational Trauma: What Is It?

When we think about trauma, we often think about painful or distressing experiences that happen directly to us. Intergenerational trauma, however, refers to the ways the effects of trauma can continue beyond the generation that originally experienced it. Unresolved emotional wounds, learned beliefs, unhealthy coping strategies, relationship patterns, and responses to fear or stress can influence children and later generations, even when they did not experience the original traumatic event themselves.

Intergenerational trauma can occur within families or entire communities and may be passed down in subtle as well as more obvious ways. Over time, these patterns can affect a person’s emotional well-being, relationships, behaviors, and even how they understand themselves and the world around them.

People experiencing intergenerational trauma may struggle with forming healthy relationships, unexplained depression or anxiety, patterns of self-sabotage or fear, or a sense of carrying a burden they struggle to name. These effects can occur in the present even when the original painful or traumatic events happened decades or generations before.

Some Examples of Intergenerational Trauma in Scripture

While the term ‘intergenerational trauma’ is something that has gained currency in recent decades, that does not mean that the reality it names is new. Scripture is quite candid about how sin has consequences; our brokenness and the brokenness of others that we endure, and experience all have consequences, and these can ripple through generations.

Two examples of this can help us. One is to consider the family of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which we read about from Genesis 12 until the end of the book. In story after story, there are repeated patterns of deeply damaging favoritism, selfishness, and deception, which cause ongoing conflict and shape the dynamics in the family across generations. In Jacob’s story, in particular, the threat of violence looms as he interacts with his brother Esau and his uncle, Laban.

Another example is David, a great king, warrior, and a man with many moral failings. After committing adultery with Bathsheba and arranging to have her husband killed, the Lord warned David that his actions would have lasting consequences in his own family (2 Samuel 11-12). David’s own son sexually assaulted his half-sister, and David did nothing about it. As a result, his family experienced even more violence and betrayal through revenge and a violent civil war.

The cycles of violence, betrayal, deception, and more that affected these families are tied to longstanding patterns of behavior that are rooted even further in the past. While this is true, Scripture also tells us that there is hope in the Lord to break such cycles.

There is the possibility of redemption, restoration, and a brand-new story for those who seek Him and pursue the new life that is possible in Him (Romans 8; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

The Causes and Triggers of Intergenerational Trauma

From what is known, intergenerational trauma has its roots in a traumatic experience a person, family, or community has. A significant event, unresolved pain, or prolonged suffering can be at the root of what goes on to become intergenerational trauma. These events could include abuse, abandonment or loss, poverty, war, forced migration, and familial patterns of violence or addiction.

These various events and experiences operate on several levels. Some of them, like experiences of war, genocide, or forced migration and displacement, are collective events that scar entire communities. Facing systemic oppression and stress from poverty and discrimination can also affect a community that is the target of such measures. There are also family dysfunctions, such as abuse, addiction, neglect, or abandonment, that can become normalized over time in a family unit.

Future generations within a community or family may not experience the original traumatic event. Still, they may inherit emotional and behavioral patterns that were formed as a response to the pain. These patterns would include anxious attachment, aggression, or deep mistrust.

Intergenerational trauma and its effects may become more noticeable during times of stress or transition. These experiences can activate learned emotional and behavioral patterns, attachment wounds, and stress responses that have been shaped by family experiences across generations.

For example, getting married or becoming a parent can trigger unresolved attachment wounds from one’s childhood or resurface old family patterns.

Other situations that may trigger this trauma include conflict situations and situations of loss and injustice that mirror those of past generations. Such conflict situations may trigger inherited anger or fears. Witnessing violence in one’s community or going through financial hardship can also activate a heightened stress response that affects one’s physical and mental well-being.

Some Signs of Intergenerational Trauma to Look Out for

Intergenerational trauma can manifest in various ways. Often, it escapes detection because it can appear as normal, and just the way your family or community does things. To pick up on how certain patterns are rooted in trauma and anything but ‘normal’ requires close examination and the willingness to make changes toward a healthier outlook. Some signs to look out for include the following:

Hypervigilance This is when you are constantly on edge, and you feel unsafe even in safe spaces.

Unhealthy relationship patterns This includes patterns of shame, denial, secrecy, mistrust, and recurring patterns of codependency.

Relational breakdown Patterns of repeated relational breakdowns across generations within the family may also point to intergenerational trauma.

Emotional problems Issues with regulating moods and emotions, persistent anxiety, depression, or emotional numbness may suggest intergenerational trauma. Also, having emotional overreactions to seemingly unrelated events could be the result of reacting to past traumas.

Inherited beliefs Carrying certain unstated or unconscious beliefs that shape your self-understanding could be a sign of intergenerational trauma. These beliefs could include feeling you are not worthy or that the world is a dangerous place. Persistent feelings of guilt or worthlessness without a clear cause may suggest intergenerational trauma.

Physical symptoms These would include insomnia, chronic pain, or stress-related conditions like heart disease.

A list of possible symptoms is a first step to help you identify what you or a loved one may be experiencing. However, various physical, emotional, and mental health challenges carry similar symptoms, and that is why it’s important to see a health professional. They can help you eliminate possible causes so that you can identify the root cause and address it.

Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma

This article started by posing a question – can we ever truly escape the past? Your past is your past, and you cannot change it. However, there is always hope for your future to look different, and to lessen the hold of the past on the here and now. There is freedom in Christ (Galatians 5:1), and with help, you can confront the past to step into a new chapter for you and your loved ones.

“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” John 8:36 ESV

The path to hope and a new future may include the following:

Acknowledge the pain Healing comes when you identify that there is a problem, a set of patterns of behaviors that are undermining the fullness of life the Lord intends for you. Reflect on your family history, naming the patterns there and recognizing how they have shaped you.

Seek the Lord’s healing You can do this through prayer, reading Scripture, and allowing Him to bring light into the dark spaces in your life. Lament is a powerful way to express your pain to the Lord, and speaking unspoken grief to the Lord in the pattern of the lament Psalms can help you find release.

Forgive and let go Forgiveness does not excuse harm; it helps you break the cycle of resentment and harm as you release the grip of the past on who you are and will be.

Set new patterns Make intentional choices empowered by God’s Spirit and grace to create new family traditions, communicate in a different style, and so on.

Seek counseling A trained Christian counselor can help you identify and unpack the deep wounds and trauma, break harmful patterns of thinking and behavior, and begin building healthier responses to everyday life.

Through faith-based counseling alongside trauma-informed therapies such as internal family systems or cognitive behavioral therapy, your counselor can help you process these deep wounds in a safe environment.

Healing the wounds of the past can start with you today. Reach out to our office or contact our reception team to connect with a counselor who can walk with you on your journey toward healing and wholeness.

References

  • Isobel, S., Goodyear, M., Furness, T., & Foster, K. (2019). Preventing intergenerational trauma transmission: A critical interpretive synthesis. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 28(7–8), 1100–1113. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.14735
  • Narayan, A. J., Lieberman, A. F., & Masten, A. S. (2021). Intergenerational transmission and prevention of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). Clinical Psychology Review, 85, 101997.

item.title: When to Seek Help for Family Problems
item.description:
Family problems can be a weight pulling you down. It can feel like taking two steps forward and three steps backward. Trying to get everyone on the same page seems fruitless at times. Whether you have babies, toddlers, grade school children, teens, or everyone in between, you want a home full of love, forgiveness, and peace. Why can’t everyone get along?

This is a fallen world, and the enemy knows where to hit the hardest to make a lasting impact: the family. Seeking help for family problems can help you get ahead and prepare you for future issues by equipping you with psychological methods and techniques, as well as faith-based principles.

Common Family Problems

Families have squabbles. Life happens, and sometimes lines are drawn in the household, but it doesn’t have to stay that way. Family problems are inevitable as personalities clash, hormones can take over, and circumstances can change on a dime. The wisdom is to get ahead of it by building a rock-solid foundation with shared beliefs and values, and open communication.

Before reading through the list of common family problems below, consider whether your family has Jesus as the cornerstone. Do you need to speak His name in normal daily conversation? Do you make decisions through a biblical lens, or do you make rash decisions that affect the entire family?

Search your heart for the answers. If you need Jesus to work on your heart and mind, ask for His forgiveness, repent, and lean on God to guide your family as the Head of the Household.

Marital Issues

Marital issues affect everyone in the family, although parents may feel that the problems lie with just the two of them. Children and teens are perceptive, and their moods and behaviors can change in response to growing fears or worries about stability. Marital issues can include emotional distance, betrayal, infidelity, financial concerns, chronic illness, procrastination, unequal household duties, and sexual intimacy problems, among others.

Marriage and family counseling are available for couples who need extra help in navigating life together. If you feel like you are alone in your marriage or that the two of you have become roommates instead of partners, seek help from a counselor.

Communications Within the Family

A communication breakdown can lead to feelings of resentment, anger, bitterness, shame, and regret. One person may push others, trying to get to the bottom of a conflict and trying to bully others to get their own way. Other family members may withdraw, becoming quiet and distant. Miscommunication leads to sibling rivalry and fights, parent-child disputes, and relationship drama between parents.

Family counseling teaches family members how to resolve conflict without insults and blaming. They learn how to manage anger and actively listen to each other. Counseling can also help spark confidence as each family member learns how to advocate for themselves.

Parenting Issues

Parenting issues include disagreements regarding discipline, sibling rivalry and fusses, and children who feel rejected, ignored, or isolated. One parent may feel that the other one contradicts them in front of the children or undermines them. Overwhelmed and stressed parents may feel like they are out of patience as they struggle to find five minutes just to think.

Problems can emerge between the two parents, divorced parents trying to co-parent, stepparents, and between parent and child. Counseling can help if every conversation feels like a struggle, or if you are only talking about surface-level topics with your teens or tweens.

Step-Parenting Adjustments

Blended families tend to have their own issues. An adjustment period is required when a parent remarries, and a new person begins living in the household. The new step-parent may have different rules or a different discipline philosophy. Parents and step-parents need to agree on how to raise the children they share.

Blended families may also include new step-siblings that change the dynamic. Children can feel neglected or ignored when other children are around. Personality clashes can also cause drama and angst in the home. Counseling equips children and parents with skills and techniques to defuse tough situations and express thoughts and emotions without resorting to insults or physical altercations.

Major Life Changes

Major life changes can turn your world upside down, sometimes for good and sometimes not. Life events can include a graduation, wedding, big move, new job, career change, pregnancy, birth of a new baby or adoption, or financial improvement. It can also include illness, death, loss of home or job, natural disaster, bankruptcy, divorce, and estrangement.

Emotional resilience builds as we face obstacles in this fallen world, but at times we may be unable to manage overwhelming blessings on our own. Counseling can help you prioritize your beliefs and values during major shifts.

Addiction

Addiction comes in many forms. You or someone in your home may struggle with addiction to alcohol, illegal drugs, prescription drugs, substances like glue or paint, pornography, sex, food, excessive shopping, or gambling. Anything that you use to fulfill a deeper need can become an addiction.

God created humans to desire Him, but because we have free will, we can reject His love or become confused. We feel an emptiness or numbness, and when we give in to an urge or impulse, we experience a temporary relief, a cascade of feel-good chemicals.

Unfortunately, unless we fill that empty hole with God, we will continue to indulge in addictions that can destroy relationships, jobs, homes, and physical and mental health. Christian counseling helps break the cycle and lean into the very One who created the heart.

Mental Health Disorders

Mental health disorders affect more than just the person experiencing them. Whether you or a family member struggles with any of the following mental health disorders, help is available.

  • Anxiety
  • Depression
  • Bipolar disorder
  • Eating disorders
  • Obsessive-compulsive disorder
  • Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
  • Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder
  • Grief
  • Cognitive disorders
  • Behavioral disorders
  • Abuse and trauma

Christian counseling centers treat families for more than just squabbles. They dive deep into mental health issues and help the family heal as a whole, while addressing their emotional and spiritual health as well.

Poor mental health affects the physical body with unexplained body aches, headaches, digestive issues, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, rapid heart rate, chronic inflammation, and increased risks of heart disease, obesity, Type II diabetes, heart attack, or stroke. Treating mental health disorders while teaching the family how to manage symptoms and work with their family member creates unity and better health.

Why Now is the Time to Seek Christian Counseling

Family problems can rob your home of peace. Now is the time to seek Christian counseling. Even if your family is not experiencing major conflict, counseling can prepare you for the inevitable. When multiple people live at home, personality clashes can arise. Teach your family how to resolve conflict and manage anger before it becomes an issue.

Sometimes families wait to seek professional help due to fear or shame. There was a time when seeking help from a counselor was ridiculed, but psychology and culture have come a long way. More people understand that it’s okay to seek help for family problems, instead of hiding them. When we try to keep problems in the dark, they seem to grow, and in families, this can create emotional distance and estrangement.

If you live in a home with abuse, self-harm, or if someone is having suicidal ideation, seek help immediately. Don’t wait. A home should be a safe haven, and we want to help you in the hard seasons.

Counseling for Family Problems

If you are leaning toward counseling for family problems, you are not alone. Our families are precious to us and deserve the best version of ourselves and to learn about how they can follow Christ while also loving one another. Contact this Christian counseling center today to schedule a session. The counselors want to help you through tough seasons with the grace and mercy of Christ.

item.title: Caring for Others Without Losing Yourself: The Importance of Caregiver Support
item.description:
There is one myth I believe many caregivers unknowingly live by. It is the belief that caring for someone else requires you to lose yourself. At first, this does not seem true. Most caregivers never wake up one morning deciding to abandon their own life. It happens little by little. It happens through responsibility. It happens through love. It happens through necessity. It happened because you took vows, and you are choosing to honor them at all costs.

Caregiving is unique because many people never choose it. It chooses them. One phone call changed everything. A stroke changes everything. It did for me. A diagnosis changes everything. It was for my mom. An accident changes everything. It does for many. Suddenly, the life you knew becomes the life you used to have.

You are no longer simply a husband, a wife, a daughter, a son. You become a caregiver; a grieving, at times confused, overwhelmed, resentful, hurt caregiver. While everyone is watching the person who is sick, few people are watching the one providing the care.

People pity caregivers, but do not support caregivers or the act of caregiving. Due to this, as one who cares for others, it is important to have key things in place to ensure you have a more pleasant experience while staying present.

Caregiving rarely begins with a choice

Most people prepare for careers. They prepare for marriage. They prepare to become parents. Few prepare to become caregivers. But I think there is room for us to start. This is a thought we will explore another time.

For those coming face to face with aging parents, you discover that one doctor’s appointment is turning into several. Hospital visits are becoming too frequent, therefore, normal. Medication schedules are replacing personal routines. Home modifications are now necessary. As the calendar slowly fills with appointments that belong to your mom or dad.

Before long, you have begun measuring each day by the needs of another person. Not to mention that you are not the one who is familiar with the doctors, and now your name is listed on official medical paperwork. You are caregiving, not just being a good son or daughter, husband or wife, friend or neighbor.

This shift happened

When someone you love or care about becomes ill, their health becomes the priority, as it should. Their recovery deserves attention. Their safety deserves protection. Their life deserves every reasonable effort. The challenge is that while their needs move to the front, yours slowly move to the back. Not because you no longer matter.

Because there never seems to be enough room for both. Why? Because family and friends who get thrust into caregiving begin giving out of necessity and panic while the knowledge of needed caregiving organization and balance is unknown to them. A caregiver in this situation does not mean to lose themselves; it just happened.

When The Sick Become the Center

Here is something that you need to know: illness naturally changes the focus of a family. Conversations become centered around symptoms. Decisions become centered around treatments. Finances become centered around medical expenses. Time becomes centered around recovery. Everything else begins to pale in comparison. Nothing seems to be more urgent. Your hobbies get put on hold. Your friendship gets put on pause. Your dreams get halted.

The caregiver often convinces themselves this is only temporary. Yet months become years. Seasons continue to change while the caregiver remains standing in the same place emotionally. This is where losing yourself quietly begins. Not through one major decision. Through thousands of small ones.

My small decisions began with seeing the need in me to bathe daily. It seemed as though when I bathed my husband, that was the most important. My needs were not. At the time of his stroke, we lived in a three-story townhome. We did not go outside for over four months. He was in prison with the punishment of the stroke, so was I.

However, I did not understand until later that he did not need me to live as if I were sick too. He needed to see me live so he could be inspired to get back to living. He wanted to see me beautified as his wife.

The Slow Disappearance of The Caregiver

This is how you know you have lost yourself as a caregiver. Losing yourself is rarely dramatic; it is more often subtle.

  • You stop asking yourself what you need.
  • You stop noticing your own exhaustion.
  • You stop celebrating your own accomplishments.
  • You stop making plans that include your own future.
  • Eventually someone asks how you are doing. Your first response is to talk about the person you care for. You no longer know how to answer the question for yourself.
  • You begin introducing yourself by someone else’s condition instead of your own life.

Watch out for this mislabeling of yourself as a caregiver. Identity is one of the first things to be disrupted as a caregiver.

  • You become the wife of the stroke survivor.
  • The husband of the spouse with cancer.
  • The daughter caring for her aging mother.
  • The son caring for his father.

These descriptions are true. They simply should not become your entire identity. There is honor in caring for others, and I do not want that to go unsaid here. Nevertheless, remember that caring for others requires you to remain able to do so.

This means that emotionally, mentally, and physically, it would be great for you to be in a stable place so that you can help from that same place. A caregiver that is inwardly secure and happy can truly go the distance in care for an individual in a pleasant and effective way. Being a caregiver is one thing; how you give care is another.

What I Wish I Had Known

As a caregiver what I wished I had known is what were some of the key tips that I needed to ensure that it was easier and how to do what was expected of me. I learned how to bathe my husband the hard way. I dressed him the hard way. I helped him use the bathroom the hard way. I fed him the hard way.

Everything I did, I will add “the hard way” because I did not know “how” to do it for a person who was disabled. This would have allowed me to save time and energy which would have helped me not to lose myself so easily in “tying” what was not the best for his condition at the time. Time and method are important.

I mentioned earlier about organization. This tags time and method for me. As a caregiver you won’t be able to get away from the tasks of what is required doctors’ visits, medication runs etc. But how you organize them is up to you. You can use delivery of medication or easier pick-up methods.

Additionally, make sure you have the medication by going to the most convenient pharmacy for you as the caregiver, not the patient. It is also wise to ensure that appointments are synced on the same day as much as possible or sprinkled throughout the week with your errands so that you and the patient are getting what you need.

Organize locations, activities, grocery trips, and leisure outings to ensure everyone gets what they need. As a caregiver, don’t forget our appointments and do not forget to schedule downtime or naps to recharge. You can do that.

Also, do not forget to schedule time to enjoy the relationship with the person and not to emphasize the duty to the person. The relationship is key to nurture while caring for them physically. I wish I had known to protect them a bit more with walks in the park, talks about emotional needs, not just physical or medical, and moments of meaningful physical touch. This includes hugs, hand-holding, kisses, etc.

The person receiving care deserves your best. Your best becomes much more difficult to give when you have nothing remaining inside yourself. Do it for them. Do it for you. Do it for the relationship.

item.title: Reframing: Changing the Way We See Our Circumstances
item.description:
While working toward my bachelor’s degree in social work, I learned a lot about reframing. “Cognitive reframing,” also known as “cognitive restructuring,” is a psychological technique that involves recognizing unhelpful or distorted thought patterns, evaluating their accuracy, and replacing them with more balanced, realistic perspectives.

In simple terms, reframing means learning to look at a situation from a different perspective. It does not mean ignoring or pretending that something difficult isn’t happening or forcing ourselves to think positively when we are hurting. Instead, it encourages us to slow down, examine the thoughts we are having, and ask whether those thoughts are completely accurate or helpful.

For example, someone might think, “I failed, so I’ll never succeed.” Cognitive reframing encourages them to pause and ask whether that thought is fully true. A more balanced perspective might be, “This setback is disappointing, but it doesn’t define my abilities or my future.”

The circumstances haven’t changed, but the interpretation has, and that shift can significantly affect how we respond to our circumstances and significantly affect our emotional well‑being.

A Brief History of Cognitive Reframing

Aaron T. Beck developed cognitive therapy in the 1960s while working with individuals experiencing depression. Through his work, Beck observed that many of his patients experienced recurring negative thoughts that influenced their emotions and behaviors. He helped patients identify these thought patterns and examine the connection between their thoughts, feelings, and actions.

Beck’s work eventually became the foundation for what is now known as cognitive restructuring. The goal is not simply to eliminate negative thoughts, but to recognize thoughts that are inaccurate, distorted, or unhelpful and replace them with healthier and more realistic perspectives.

In other words, we don’t necessarily have to believe every thought that enters our minds. That concept has always fascinated me, particularly because it connects with something the Bible has been teaching for centuries: the importance of being intentional about what we allow to occupy our minds.

Our Thoughts Matter

I love listening to Dr. Caroline Leaf, a cognitive neuroscientist, communication pathologist, and author who has written extensively about thoughts, emotions, and mental health. Her work has encouraged many people to become more intentional about examining their thoughts and the meaning they assign to their experiences.

One of the ideas she discusses is that we have a choice in how we respond to the information that enters our minds. We are constantly receiving information from the outside world through conversations, social media, news, relationships, and our circumstances. At the same time, we are also dealing with thoughts and memories that we already have.

We cannot always control what thoughts initially enter our minds. A fearful thought may suddenly appear. A painful memory may resurface. Someone may say something hurtful to us. We may experience a setback and immediately begin telling ourselves a story about what that setback means. But we can become more intentional about what we do with those thoughts.

Do we automatically accept the thought as truth? Do we replay it over and over? Or do we stop and examine it? This is where reframing becomes practical.

Taking Our Thoughts Captive

As Christians, we have an additional framework for examining our thoughts. In 2 Corinthians 10:5, Paul reinforces this by urging believers to “take every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.”

We don’t have to allow every thought to run freely through our minds. It is about recognizing when our thoughts drift toward fear, hopelessness, distortion, or self‑condemnation – and intentionally replacing them with what is true. “Fix your thoughts on what is true, and honorable, and right, and pure, and lovely, and admirable. Think about things that are excellent and worthy of praise” Philippians 4:8 (NLT).

We can stop and ask questions such as:

  • Is this thought true?
  • Is this thought helpful?
  • Am I assuming something that I don’t actually know?
  • Does this thought line up with what God says?
  • What would a more balanced perspective look like?

Sometimes our thoughts are based on fear, past experiences, insecurity, or assumptions rather than truth. Reframing gives us a practical way to slow down and examine those thoughts rather than allowing them to control our emotions and behavior.

Renewing Our Minds

The Bible also tells us that we are to renew our minds. Dr. Leaf says if we choose to dwell on thoughts – by analyzing it, meditating on it, or giving it meaning – it becomes part of our memory networks. Once embedded, it must be rebuilt, which she connects to the biblical concept of renewing the mind.

Romans 12:2 says, “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” What we continually focus on, repeatedly tell, or meditate on matters.

This doesn’t mean that Christians should ignore problems or pretend that life is always good. Scripture certainly doesn’t teach us to deny pain. Instead, it teaches us where to place our attention when we are walking through difficult circumstances.

We can acknowledge, “This is hard,” while also reminding ourselves, “God is with me.” Jesus said, “I have told you these things, so that in me you may have peace. In this world you will have trouble. But take heart! I have overcome the world” (John 16:33, NIV).

We can say, “I don’t know how this is going to work out,” while also saying, “I know I don’t have to face it alone. God will work it out. And even if it doesn’t work out the way I wanted, God will work everything for good (Romans 8:28).” We can recognize disappointment without allowing disappointment to become our identity. That is the difference between simply “thinking positively” and renewing our minds.

A Personal Example

I have experienced the power of reframing in my own life. When my husband and I first moved to Western Washington from Southeast Idaho, I complained about the price of our apartment. Many of my friends back in Idaho were paying approximately the same amount for their mortgages on newly built homes as we were paying in rent for a two-bedroom apartment. I found it difficult to feel content.

Then one night, when I couldn’t sleep, I turned on the television. I was watching a program that showed young families living in extreme poverty. They didn’t have clean water or indoor plumbing, and had little food.

I looked around our apartment. We had clean water. We had indoor plumbing. We had food. We had a comfortable place to sleep. We even had a gas fireplace that I loved to put on at night. Nothing about my circumstances had changed.

The apartment was exactly the same, but suddenly, my perspective was different. God helped me change my perspective. For the first time, instead of focusing on what I didn’t have, I recognized how much I did have. I felt rich.

Over the years, I have had to remind myself to put on my figurative “rose-colored glasses” and look at my circumstances through new eyes. That doesn’t mean ignoring reality. It means intentionally looking for another perspective.

What Are We Choosing to Focus On?

1 Thessalonians 5 encourages us to rejoice, pray continually, and give thanks in all circumstances. That doesn’t mean we will enjoy every circumstance we experience. It means that even in difficult circumstances, we can look for reasons to remain connected to God and practice gratitude. James 1:2 tells us to “count it all joy when you fall into various trials.” The NLT says, “when troubles of any kind come your way.”

This is one reason gratitude can be such a powerful practice.

When we are overwhelmed, our attention can become completely consumed by what is going wrong. Reframing helps us widen the lens.

  • What else is true?
  • What am I overlooking?
  • What am I grateful for? (I often suggest starting a gratitude journal).
  • What does God say about me?
  • What can I learn from this?
  • Where do I see God working?

Sometimes changing our perspective doesn’t change the circumstance. It changes us as we walk through the circumstance.

Second Timothy 1:7 reminds us that God has given us a spirit of power, love, and a sound mind. Philippians 2:3-4 also encourages us to look beyond ourselves and consider the needs of others.

Sometimes the best way to interrupt our own negative thought cycle is to take our eyes off ourselves and refocus them on God and others.

We Can Choose a Different Perspective

We will all experience disappointment, fear, loss, frustration, and circumstances we wish we could change. We will also have thoughts that are discouraging, fearful, or simply untrue. The goal isn’t to never have a negative thought. The goal is to notice it, pause, examine it, and then decide whether it deserves to stay.

Cognitive reframing gives us a practical tool for challenging unhelpful thinking and developing a more balanced perspective. As Christians, we can take that practice one step further by asking whether our thoughts align with the truth of God’s Word.

We may not always be able to choose what happens to us. We may not be able to control every thought that enters our minds. But we can become more intentional about what we dwell on, what we believe, and where we choose to focus our attention.

Next Steps

Changing perspective doesn’t always require changing circumstances. Sometimes, it simply requires seeing those circumstances through new eyes.

If you struggle with negative thoughts, automatic thoughts, or cognitive distortions, we have wonderful Christian counselors who can help you learn how to stop them and replace them. Counselors help overcome cognitive distortions through structured therapeutic approaches like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and cognitive restructuring.
